text:
INTRODUCTION
The UEFA Technical Observer Group
provided comprehensive coverage
of the action as the UEFA Champions
League entered a new era in 2024/25
This review of the 2024/25 UEFA Champions League season covers
a campaign that featured a new format as the September-January
league phase replaced the September-December group stage. It
involved an additional four teams – up from 32 to 36 – and meant
that the overall number of matches rose to 189, the last of which
was the final at the Munich Football Arena on 31 May.
To assess the action, the UEFA Technical Observer Group worked
together with the UEFA performance analysis unit from September
through to May. An observer was assigned to analyse each fixture
from Matchday 1 onwards, with one present in the stadium for
every fixture in the knockout stage. Their insights have informed the
assessment of the tactical approach of each participating club as
well as the broader points addressed.

It involved an additional four teams – up from 32 to 36 – and meant that the overall number of matches rose to 189, the last of which was the final at the Munich Football Arena on 31 May. To assess the action, the UEFA Technical Observer Group worked together with the UEFA performance analysis unit from September through to May. An observer was assigned to analyse each fixture from Matchday 1 onwards, with one present in the stadium for every fixture in the knockout stage. Their insights have informed the assessment of the tactical approach of each participating club as well as the broader points addressed.

This section explores how restarts were used to progress the ball,
manipulate pressing structures and create space – with standout
examples from Lille, Manchester City and Bayern München. An
analysis of the total of 2,581 goal kicks across the campaign found
that almost one quarter (24%) were taken by an outfield player.
Starting goal kicks with a centre-back rather than the goalkeeper
has become increasingly common and was observed frequently during
this season’s UEFA Champions League. When the centre-back initiates
play, opponents typically respond by locking on to nearby outfield
options to prepare a pressing trap, rather than directly applying
pressure on the goalkeeper, who is typically positioned centrally.
Pressing the goalkeeper centrally may allow space to an outfield player
instead and with it comes the risk of being exposed behind the first
line of pressure. For the side building play, meanwhile, it allows the
keeper more time on the ball and is a strategy that can be helpful for
coping with player-to-player pressure.

INTRODUCTION

The 2024/25 UEFA Women’s Champions League report provides in-depth analysis and
key discussion points focusing on the technical and tactical trends from this season’s
competition.
Matches from the group stage through to the final in Lisbon on 24 May have been
analysed by UEFA’s Technical Observer Group. This process, which utilises UEFA’s
latest technological innovations, has prompted a wealth of fascinating insight and
discussion summarised in this report.
This year’s competition has further highlighted the continued evolution of elite
women’s football across Europe. Many teams and individuals have contributed to a
thoroughly engaging competition, which has been notable for numerous excellent
attacking performances as well as some standout defensive displays. A number of
these impressive individual performances have been captured in our comprehensive
awards section covering Team of the Season, Player of the Season, Young Player of the
Season and Top Scorer. The top ten goals of the competition are also listed.

DOUBLE CHANGE TURNS THE TIDE
Arsenal’s 1-0 victory over Barcelona in the final of the
2024/25 UEFA Women’s Champions League owed much
to the introduction of second-half substitutes Stina
Blackstenius and Beth Mead. With the game locked
at 0-0 and Barcelona increasingly building attacking
momentum, Arsenal coach Renée Slegers made a
decisive double change that would shift the rhythm of the
game and give the north London side their first European
trophy in 18 years.
With 67 minutes played, Slegers withdrew forwards
Frida Maanum and Chloe Kelly, introducing Blackstenius
and Mead from the bench. The changes triggered a small
tactical adjustment that would prove crucial in deciding
who would lift the trophy in Lisbon. As part of the
reshuffle, Arsenal centre-forward Alessia Russo, who had
worked tirelessly at the top of the pitch, dropped into the
deeper position previously occupied by Maanum. With
Russo now looking to connect the game from a more
withdrawn position, Blackstenius was free to work up
against Barcelona’s back line.

defended,” added Signeul. “Arsenal were aware
of what Barcelona wanted to do and then stayed
together and worked so hard to defend against it.
The hard work they put in was very impressive.”

Bayern München made an impressive start to their
2024/25 Women’s Champions League campaign with a
5-2 win over Arsenal on Matchday 1. Building from the back
was integral to this display from Alexander Straus’ team,
who demonstrated their intent to play through the thirds
of the pitch during what was a comprehensive victory.
Deep-lying midfielder Georgia Stanway, operating
as one of two Bayern midfield pivots, played a central
role in the German side’s build-up play. The England
international routinely moved away from central areas to
a wider position behind Arsenal’s two central attackers as
they attempted to press high. The benefit of Stanway’s
movement was twofold: either she found space to receive
and start an attack from a wide position, or she tempted
an Arsenal player away from the central area to open up
a passing lane. With Bayern forward Pernille Harder keen
to drop into the spaces vacated by Stanway, the hosts
cleverly found ways to play through Arsenal’s press.

text:
WIDE PLAYERS MAKE THEIR MARK
Wide attackers were the most prolific scorers in the competition,
registering 69 goals, one more than centre-forwards. That closeness
in numbers highlights both the evolving role of the wide player and
the centre-forward as well as the fluidity of attacking movement
adopted by many of the competition’s best teams.
Lyon’s Kadidiatou Diani, Melchie Dumornay and Tabitha Chawinga,
who scored 14 goals between them, were one example of a forward
line who regularly interchanged positions. As a result, it was often
the wide players who moved inside into central goalscoring areas.
“We've worked a lot on it at training,” explained Lyon head coach
Joe Montemurro. “If they stay in position, it's a lot easier to read
so they are the ones in the moment to identify the space. One will
come short and take a defender away, another one will go over the
top or come inside. So they have this autonomy and effectively they
understand where the space is in the moments.”

KEY FOR ARSENAL
Goal kicks taken by central defender Leah Williamson were a key
feature of Arsenal’s build-up play in the final against Barcelona. The
England captain regularly initiated play from goal kicks, either passing
short to goalkeeper Daphne van Domselaar or playing further forward
into Arsenal’s front line.
With Barcelona intent on pressing high from Arsenal’s goal kicks,
Williamson’s variety kept their opponents guessing as to where
the next pass would be delivered. If Williamson played short to her
goalkeeper, Barcelona’s attackers were unsure whether to press and
leave the two centre-backs. Similarly, by encouraging the opposition
to press high, Williamson also had the option to play over the high
press and directly into the front line.
How Arsenal varied their build-up play in the final was a
key feature of Renée Slegers’ side’s approach.

Possessing attacking players who have the ability to repeatedly
run in behind the opposition back line proved a crucial strategy for
creating chances in the knockout stages.
The willingness of Barcelona’s attackers to perform this action,
linked with their ability to play accurate forward passes, was a
successful attacking strategy for the Spanish side. Barcelona attacker
Ewa Pajor registered 105 runs in behind during the season, the most
in the competition – Arsenal forward Alessia Russo was second on
61 – with her club having six goal actions as a result.
Barcelona winger Fridolina Rolfö was another source of attacking
runs, the Swedish international proving efficient when she did move
beyond the opposition back line. On 44% of occasions, Rolfö’s runs
led to her team finishing the play with a shot at goal.
Lyon forward Melchie Dumornay also proved effective when
running in behind, contributing to four goals for her side.

team because there is limited reaction time. Also, in these situations,

A total of 77 goals were scored from open-play crosses in the
2024/25 UEFA Women’s Champions League. Barcelona and Lyon
benefited most, scoring 14 and 12 goals respectively. Both sides
also registered the highest number of crosses in a match with 19.
Barcelona demonstrated their threat in wide areas during their
4-1 semi-final second-leg victory at Chelsea. In the clip below
the Spanish side worked the ball onto the right of the attack,
where wide attacker Caroline Graham beats her opponent before
delivering a low cross for attacker Ewa Pajor to score with a first-
time finish.

delivered from areas outside the width of the penalty box, Graham
Hansen’s delivery from inside the penalty area also highlighted
another common route to goal. Across the competition, one in three
crosses were delivered from inside the penalty area. Notably, for
both crosses inside and outside of the box, the right of the attack
was preferred over the left.

REGAINS INTO GOALS
Lyon’s ability to regain the ball in the attacking third was a key
feature of their run to the semi-finals. Joe Montemurro’s side
registered the highest number of regains in the attacking third per
game with 25; as a result, they created ten opportunities per game
from the regains. This pressing approach led to 12 goals for the
French side, a figure bettered only by Barcelona who scored 16.
Integral to this approach was the high-press approach of
attackers Kadidiatou Diani and Melchie Dumornay, who ranked
among the top players for attacking-third regains. Young Player
of the Season Dumornay impressed with her attitude, application
and technique in regaining the ball in the attacking third. The Haiti
international registered the highest number of attacking-third
regains with 38.
The French side used the physical qualities of Dumornay and
Lindsey Heaps to support attacker Ada Hegerberg in applying
pressure to the opposition back line.

MANCHESTER CITY EXCEL
Manchester City’s effective use of a mid-block to prevent opponents
penetrating was a standout feature of their run to the quarter-
finals. Overall 44% of the English side’s ball recoveries occurred in
the middle third, averaging 27 mid-block regains per game. Their
efficiency in this aspect of the game was underlined during their
group stage fixture against St. Pölten, when they recorded 42 mid-
block regains – the highest of the season.
In total 36% of City’s mid-third regains came in central areas,
a figure matched only by Barcelona. Crucial to City’s work in this
area of the pitch was the contribution of Japanese international
midfielder Yui Hasegawa, who recorded the most mid-third ball
recoveries in the competition with 46. Given City played three
fewer games than finalists Arsenal and Barcelona, Hasegawa’s work
in this area was significant.
In the clips Hasegawa demonstrates the importance of
awareness, anticipation and speed of movement when
intercepting passes.

WIDE TO REGAIN
Arsenal adopted a different approach to Manchester City when
attempting to recover the ball in the middle third of the pitch. Where
City looked to regain in central areas, Arsenal remained compact
with the aim of forcing their opposition wide. Just 29% of Renée
Slegers’s side’s mid-block regains came from the centre of the mid-
block, whereas 71% were made in wide areas.
“Arsenal worked so hard to stay compact and press the ball in
good positions,” explained Martin Sjögren, UEFA Technical Observer,
following their 4-1 victory over Lyon in the semi-final second leg.
“They have really good defensive structure and compactness. They
were on the front foot throughout the game and won a lot of duels.”
Arsenal regularly adopted a 4-4-2 shape in their mid-block with
important contributions from their two highest attacking players.
“Arsenal defended in a 4-4-2 mid-block with the aim of moving
out of the mid-block to a high press. They were compact and used
zonal defending,” explained Sjögren.

form a back three with a holding midfielder in front.”

PREVENTING CHANCES: OPEN PLAY
Goalkeepers helped prevent goalscoring opportunities by going
through a process of observation, positional adjustment and
decision-making, according to UEFA’s technical experts.
“During Real Madrid’s quarter-final second leg against Arsenal,
the positional play of Misa was excellent,” explained Stewart and
Vencel. “She was organising and communicating with her defenders.
When Arsenal’s Chloe Kelly delivered a dangerous low narrow cross
between defenders and goalkeeper, Misa made a good decision
to deal with the cross and made a brave, effective save stopping
potential danger to her goal.”
Wolfsburg goalkeeper Anneke Borbe demonstrated a similar
process of observation, positional adjustment and decision-making
in the German side’s quarter-final first leg versus Barcelona.

understanding and effective relationships between goalkeeper

effective communicators in order to take responsibility in these

VARYING LEVEL OF INVOLVEMENT
When analysing goalkeeping performances in the
2024/25 UEFA Women’s Champions League, UEFA’s
technical experts assessed different types of involvement
and actions:
Regular involvement: Occurs where imminent
involvement with the ball is unlikely. The goalkeeper is in
observation and communication mode and takes up a
position relative to team shape
High involvement: Includes actively supporting and
preparing the execution of a particular team task
Ball involvement: When the goalkeeper is required to
be directly involved with the ball (e.g. handling, passing,
1v1 situation, putting pressure on the ball)

text:
DEFENDING THE GOAL
A goalkeeper’s ability to make important saves had a major
impact on the match outcome from the quarter-finals onwards,
said UEFA’s goalkeeping experts. “The goalkeeper must have
high involvement through preparation in order to increase the
probability of making a save in demanding situations,” explained
Stewart and Vencel. “In general, at this level when teams of similar
strengths are competing and matches are in the balance, the
importance of the goalkeepers’ action to defending the goal has,
and will always be, the prime objective.
“To achieve this, the goalkeeper follows the same basic sequence:
observe events on the pitch; collect information and compare it
with previous experiences; select key aspects; decide how to act by
reacting to situational cues; execute the action appropriately.”
Both Arsenal’s Van Domselaar and Barcelona’s Coll
demonstrated excellent examples of defending the goal on the
way to the final. During Arsenal’s quarter-final second leg with
Real Madrid, Van Domselaar and the Arsenal defence recovered
and adjusted to defend against Real’s overload in the wide area.

This was the first UEFA Europa League under the new format, with
a 36-team league phase replacing the previous 32-team group
stage. Excluding qualifying rounds, the total number of matches in
the competition increased from 141 to 189, with the final played at
the San Mamés Stadium in Bilbao.

of the 55 UEFA member nations participated and the 36 who
contested the league phase featured 13 former UEFA Cup/
Europa Legue finalists and six winners, among them Eintracht
Frankfurt and Manchester United, who had lifted the trophy
as recently as 2022 and 2017 respectively. The latter were the
highest-placed (11th) in the UEFA club rankings, heading 30
teams who appeared in the continent’s top 100. The lowest-
placed participants were Elfsborg of Sweden, ranked 302 and
who, along with Ferencváros of Hungary and Latvia’s RFS, edged
into the league phase via penalty shoot-outs in the play-off
round, while Olympiacos of Greece qualified as winners of the
2023/24 UEFA Conference League.

lying midfielder.

GROUND TIPS
Steve Cooper,
UEFA Technical Observer
Preparing a defensive plan
Off the pitch, you can show how you’re going to defend in certain
areas – showing clips and using the tactics board. On the training
pitch you might walk through scenarios but also try to create game-
like situations, such as putting the opposition shape against your
shape and recreating possible passing tactical moves that can be
deployed by the opposition.
When you coach these real-life scenarios, there are always ‘what-
ifs’ arising. What if the full-back doesn’t get pressure on the ball? The
wingers aren’t in a position to defend the inside? That’s when you’re
able to talk about the trade-off between what you’re willing to give up
and what you’re hoping to do.
When it comes to practice design, you might zone off the pitch with
certain players only going in areas to mimic the opposition’s shape
and passing sequences. If you’re working on the high press, you might
use half the pitch, with the opposition trying to get over the halfway
line.

Free-kicks
There were only five successes from direct free-kicks
over the course of the season’s 189 games. Goals from
indirect free-kicks were less of a rarity, Manchester
United and Ajax notching three apiece to lead the
field. But Eintracht Frankfurt’s second goal in the 3-1
away win against Beşiktaş stood out as a creative,
well-rehearsed set play. A free-kick was played to
Omar Marmoush, whose curling right-footed diagonal
was nodded by Robin Koch into the middle of the box
where the unmarked Dina Ebimbe side-footed past the
goalkeeper.
“A set-piece routine like this demands flawless timing
and technical excellence,” said Jan Peder Jalland,
UEFA Technical Observer. “Frankfurt strategically
split their front five during the free-kick from the
centre, positioning players to exploit both left and
right channels. In this instance, they chose the
shorter route – a quick pass from slightly right to the
left, followed by an inswinging cross. This approach
created advantageous angles while posing significant
challenges for the Beşiktaş defence.”

text:
THE COACHES
The UEFA Coaching Convention sets minimum
standards for national associations and offers
them guidance, information and support
The UEFA Coaching Convention provides a benchmark
for the education of coaches within Europe, helping to
raise the quality of coaching across the continent and
facilitating the free movement of qualified professionals
around UEFA’s member associations. The value of Article
8 of the convention is worth highlighting as it promotes
reality-based learning – a key tool for coaches today.
Informal learning
UEFA supports informal learning – learning that is incidental
or self-directed and not led by another person. Examples
include everyday experiences, observing or talking to other
coaches and self-study. The more insights coaches gain,
the better they can discover what works for them in practice.
Understanding how to apply knowledge in coaching is a key
part of development.

Preparing for game-realistic
scenarios
These can be structured moments such as patterns of
play and help coaches build a game model and develop
player understanding of key principles. Structured practice
provides more control to create the pictures they want to
see but should not restrict decision-making. Opposition
analysis can offer insight, but coaches must adapt to
challenges on matchday. This may involve tactical changes
or substitutions. In the UEFA Conference League final,
Chelsea coach Enzo Maresca introduced Jadon Sancho,
a winger who dribbles and drives forward. As Church
said: “He makes the defence drop, which is a different
tactical problem.”
Coaches should create environments where players
identify problems and find solutions. Kris Van Der Haegen,
coach education director at the Belgian FA, said: “You need
to give them the space to try out what they have. If they
recognise the structure of the opposition and they know
their role, they can express themselves in a creative way.”
Unstructured moments such as transition are harder to
prepare for.

Cole Palmer in control
Palmer sparks Chelsea recovery

that had propelled Chelsea to the final as runaway leading scorers
in the competition with 38 goals – eight more than their nearest
rivals, Fiorentina.
A combination of personnel changes – starting with Reece James
replacing right-back Malo Gusto at half-time – and the belated
emergence of their own creator-in-chief, Cole Palmer, turned the game
on its head in dramatic fashion. “I was sick of getting the ball and going
backwards or sideways,” explained Palmer. “I thought, ‘When I next get
the ball, I’m just going to go [forward]’ – and it worked.”
The Chelsea No10 replaced Isco as the outstanding player on the
pitch by setting up two goals in six minutes. “Palmer delivered two
moments of magic that transformed the contest,” said Adams.

LEAGUE PHASE
The 2024/25 UEFA Conference League began with a new 36-team
league phase, marking a significant shift from the previous group
stage structure as clubs competed in a single league table. Each team
played six fixtures – three at home and three away – resulting in an
increase from 96 to 108 matches.
The top eight teams in the league phase advanced directly to
the round of 16, while those ranked from ninth to 24th entered the
knockout phase play-offs, with the ninth to 16th-placed teams given
home advantage for the second leg. The teams placed 25th to 36th
ended their campaigns at the conclusion of the league phase.
Former UEFA Champions League winners Chelsea proved their
credentials by registering six wins out of six to take top spot. The
English side, the highest-ranked team in the UEFA coefficient,
conceded only five times and racked up 26 goals, including an 8-0 rout
of the club with the lowest UEFA coefficient ranking, Armenian Premier
League runners-up Noah.

pass from a retreating midfielder.

become a key strategic phase in modern football. Across the
2024/25 UEFA Conference League, teams demonstrated
tactical variation in how they initiated possession, whether
playing short to bait pressure or launching directly to bypass it.

approach, using an outfield player to take the restart, was
typically reserved for situations involving aggressive player-
to-player pressing from high opponents. In these cases, the
goalkeeper remained central while the defender initiated play.

for the education of coaches within Europe, helping to
raise the quality of coaching across the continent and
facilitating the free movement of qualified professionals

reality-based learning – a key tool for coaches today.
Informal learning

or self-directed and not led by another person. Examples
include everyday experiences, observing or talking to other
coaches and self-study. The more insights coaches gain,
the better they can discover what works for them in practice.
Understanding how to apply knowledge in coaching is a key
part of development.

Preparing for game-realistic
scenarios
These can be structured moments such as patterns of
play and help coaches build a game model and develop
player understanding of key principles. Structured practice
provides more control to create the pictures they want to
see but should not restrict decision-making. Opposition
analysis can offer insight, but coaches must adapt to
challenges on matchday. This may involve tactical changes
or substitutions. In the UEFA Conference League final,
Chelsea coach Enzo Maresca introduced Jadon Sancho,
a winger who dribbles and drives forward. As Church
said: “He makes the defence drop, which is a different
tactical problem.”
Coaches should create environments where players
identify problems and find solutions. Kris Van Der Haegen,
coach education director at the Belgian FA, said: “You need
to give them the space to try out what they have. If they
recognise the structure of the opposition and they know
their role, they can express themselves in a creative way.”
Unstructured moments such as transition are harder to
prepare for.

UEFA’s Technical Observer Group were on hand to
analyse all the action as the tournament continued
to reach new heights on and off the pitch
This review of UEFA Women’s EURO 2025 provides a record of a
tournament which comprised 31 matches across 26 days between
2 and 27 July 2025.
Held in eight venues across Switzerland, this was the third 16-
team Women’s EURO final tournament and it had the tagline ‘The
summit of emotions’ – which proved fitting given the way it took
the women’s game in Europe to fresh heights.
With an overall attendance of 657,291 and 29 of the 31 fixtures
sold out, the finals set a record for spectators at a Women’s EURO
while on the pitch there were an unprecedented number of goals
scored – a total of 106 at a rate of 3.42 per game.
And it ended with Sarina Wiegman’s England becoming the
second team after Germany to win back-to-back Women’s
EUROs thanks to their final triumph over world champions Spain.

come up against a low block.”

text:
MAKING CROSSING COUNT
"Effective crossing play demands the following
attributes: speed and decision-making to exploit
space; detail and variability of delivery – i.e. cutback,
flat, lofted, driven; and good movement, with the
right disguise and timing to attack the cross.
"Attacking players should have areas to target
based on where the delivery comes from and from
whom – be it a right- or left-footed player – and
there are other obvious components for a coach to
bear in mind, such as finishing, heading and blockers.
"On the training pitch, we'd focus on a range
of aspects: getting into position to cross, which
involves combination play, 1v1s, positioning;
delivery; attacking the first phase and anticipating
the second phase. On this last point, we'd anticipate
areas for delivery based on where the ball comes
from. From the touchline, you'd expect a cutback,
while if it's an early break behind the back line,
then you'd anticipate a flat or driven cross behind
the retreating defence.

text:
YIELDS LATE REWARD
Germany showed impressive cohesion and resilience
in frustrating the tournament’s top scorers for 113
minutes of a compelling semi-final in Zurich. Operating
mostly in a compact 1-4-5-1 mid-block, they applied
quick, consistent pressure on the ball-carrier and made
it hard for Spain to play through them.
If challenged by Germany’s high press, Montse
Tomé’s side kept to their attacking style and, in
opposition territory, they displayed a controlled
attacking approach which bore fruit eventually with
Aitana Bonmatí’s strike.
Appraising Spain’s approach, UEFA Technical
Observer Irene Fuhrmann said: “In possession, they
always create short passing options nearby to keep
the ball moving and shift the opponent, in order to
then play vertically.
“Especially on the flanks, the full-backs frequently
overlap the midfielders to create numerical
superiority or exploit the space that has been opened
up. One tactic they often use is the third-player
combination – with an open body position and a run
behind the defensive line, they repeatedly create
dangerous situations.”

Central to Spain’s attacking approach, added
Fuhrmann, was an individual and collective focus on
creating and exploiting space. Before her goal, for
example, Aitana could be seen scanning, standing still,
as well as adjusting her position by moving backwards,

pocket of space.

them and, even without the ball, know how to get free
at the right moment or draw defenders away to open
up space,” explained Fuhrmann. “They create space
by circulating the ball within their own team and by
positioning themselves well in the gaps, in the spaces
between the lines, or by making dynamic runs in behind
to demand balls played beyond the defensive line.
“In addition, the Spain players are very strong in
1v1 situations. They can beat their opponents using
body feints and changes of pace when dribbling, or
they move intelligently out of their opponent’s line of
sight to find open positions between the lines.”

HOW THE GOALS WERE SCORED
The way that the goals were scored in Switzerland offered further
encouraging signs about the technical advances made in the
women’s game. With 80% of goals sourced from open play, there
was less reliance on set plays than at the 2022 tournament.
Then, 26% of the goals came via free-kicks and corners; this
time, they accounted for 12%.
“We’ve improved in terms of technical skills,” said UEFA
Technical Observer Lluís Cortés as he praised the quality of
the goals and noted the shrinking number that had come from
opposition errors.
The majority of open-play goals came against opponents
defending in a low block, with the team having to engineer a way
through, often via combination plays.

Germany succeeded in keeping out the tournament’s highest

maintaining tight distances between the units.

1-4-3-3, with UEFA Technical Observer Irene Fuhrmann explaining:
“Germany’s wide midfielders, Klara Bühl and Jule Brand,
often pushed higher up against Spain’s back three, positioning
themselves almost on the same line as the striker.
“They kept a tight formation to make it difficult for Spain to
play through the centre or between the lines. If the ball was
played to the Spain wingers, Brand and Bühl tracked back to
support their full-backs. Deep runs from Spain’s midfielders were
tracked consistently.”
The role of striker Giovanna Hoffmann is worth highlighting
too for the way she applied pressure on the player on the ball.

to Lucy Bronze at the moment the England right-back intercepted
a loose pass. As UEFA Technical Observer Britta Carlson observed:

rhythm when they regained possession because Spain counter-
pressed so effectively after losing it.”

possession and structure effectively to prevent counterattacks”. In
other words, their positioning enabled them to win the ball back
quickly and attack again, helping them dictate play.
Pivotal to this was holding midfielder Patri Guijarro, as UEFA
Technical Observer Lluís Cortés explained. “Many times she
recovers the ball,” he said.

goalkeepers dealt well with crosses to the near post and to the

cutbacks presented difficulties at times, as did crosses to the far

and closest defender – their position in the goal and set position
didn’t allow them to dive and intercept the ball. The goalkeepers
are thinking much more about the second ball. We think this needs
deeper analysis.”

According to the UEFA Goalkeeper Expert Group, the
growing technical ability of elite players has increased the
risk of goalkeepers being caught out when taking up high
starting positions. “There were two or three examples
during the tournament,” they said. “The positional play of
the goalkeeper is evolving and adjusting to the demands
of the game and team principles to play higher, but
more players are capable of delivering a long, 50m pass
exposing the position of the goalkeeper.”

For the experts, there was no better example than Germany
goalkeeper Berger’s wonderful backward save in the quarter-
final against France. “This is the perfect example of the fact that
female goalkeeping has also reached the top level,” said the
UEFA Goalkeeper Experts, adding that Berger had initially been
anticipating a “central high cross” into the penalty area, as shown
in the image to the right of her pointing to the coming threat.
When Janina Minge’s inadvertent header sent the ball in the
opposite direction – arcing over the goalkeeper’s head – Berger
“acted without hesitation, switching quickly and saving the ball in
an exceptional manner”.

SHOOT-OUTS
The UEFA Goalkeeper Experts found a positive too in some of the
goalkeeping displays in penalty shoot-outs. While acknowledging
that “numerous missed penalties naturally raises the question of
whether the shooters were particularly bad or the goalkeepers
particularly good,” they saw encouraging signs in the goalkeepers’
efforts. Hampton and Coll each made two saves in the final shoot-
out, for example, while Berger excelled in the quarter-final against
France, stopping two kicks and converting one herself.
The UEFA Goalkeeper Experts identified the following aspects of
the goalkeepers’ work in these situations:
• Their homework was done in detail, e.g. preparation of penalty takers,
shooting patterns, creative visualisation (water bottles, arm notes etc)
• Fitness levels were high as these goalkeepers are now professional
athletes who can play for 120+ minutes every few days
• Mental strength was evident during these periods of pressure,
with leadership and strong personalities revealed in small
moments, e.g. England’s Hampton handing over the ball to
their next penalty taker to avoid any distraction from the Spain
goalkeeper in the final.

FITNESS
The UEFA Fitness Group put the teams’ physical data under
the microscope, with high-intensity output up significantly and
some marked variations according to position and tactics
Towards the end of her press conference after England’s final
victory, Sarina Wiegman began a reflection that went beyond
her own team’s exploits to touch on broader tournament
trends. And it was telling that she soon landed on the physical
aspect of the matches in Switzerland, declaring: “The intensity
of the games went through the roof.”
That assertion from the winning coach of the last three
Women’s EUROs aligned with the view of the UEFA Technical
Observer Group, with Anna Signeul highlighting this aspect
when she said: “I’ve been immensely impressed by the
intensity of the games and the fitness level of the players. In
the three years since the previous EURO, the fitness level has
increased very much.”
Intensity is the apposite word. The average total distance
covered per player at this tournament was actually lower
than in 2022 yet high-intensity output increased.

positional physical demands but to consider the unique positional
requirements of zone 5 running in and out of possession when
designing training drills.

text:
COMBINATIONS
Session organisation
• 19 players total: 9 attackers + GK (Orange), 7 defenders + GK (Purple)
and 1 neutral player (always supports team in possession)
• Set up a pitch divided into three vertical zones (A–B–C)
• The Orange team (9 players) always start in possession
• Neutral player supports the team in possession and can move freely
across zones
• Rules for Orange (in possession):
- If the ball travels from Zone A to Zone B, the players in Zone B must
return the ball to Zone A (to attract pressure)
- If the ball goes directly from Zone A to Zone C, players in Zone C must
combine with a third-player action via Zone B before freely attacking
- Once a third-player combination is achieved through Zone B, Zone B
players can join the attack into Zone C
• Rules for Purple (out of possession):
- Defenders can move freely across all zones
- Upon regaining possession, their objective is to counterattack
and score as quickly as possible
